title: How food reaches us, and how the body fights germs
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 4 Chapter 6 'Happy and Healthy Living' (journey of a grain and gratitude; not wasting food; mindful eating, exercise and rest; a safe environment) and Cambridge Stage 4 Biology Unit 1.5 'Medicines and infectious diseases' (taking medicines safely; germs and infectious diseases; vaccination past and present). No textbook needed.
summary: A single meal needs soil, rain, sun, earthworms, farmers, millers, drivers and cooks. Your child follows a grain of rice from the field to the stomach, and finds that digestion begins in the mouth. They count the food their family throws away and ask how much is enough. Then they learn how the body defends itself against germs, how a vaccine teaches the body to recognise a germ, and how vaccines protect even people who are not vaccinated. They learn to use medicines safely. They meet an enslaved African man in Boston, the inoculators of Bengal, a Chinese scientist who searched old books for a malaria cure, and 'Mouldy Mary', who found a better penicillin mould on a market melon.
builds_on: Class 2: food builds the body, germs and soap, heartbeat and exercise, teeth. Class 3: caring for every outer organ, clean surroundings, three kinds of fitness, rest and sleep, my body belongs to me. Here: the journey of food and digestion, food waste, the immune system, vaccines and medicines. Class 5 goes on to how particular diseases spread (water, air, mosquitoes), non-infectious diseases, and how towns and countries stop epidemics.
goals: By the end your child can tell the journey of a grain from seed to plate and name the living things and people it depends on.
By the end your child can explain that digestion starts in the mouth, and practise mindful eating.
By the end your child can measure their family's food waste and suggest ways to waste less.
By the end your child can explain how the body defends itself against germs and how a vaccine trains it to remember a germ.
By the end your child can explain how vaccines protect a whole community, and state the rules for using medicines safely, including why antibiotics don't work on viruses.

days.title: The journey of a grain
days.goal: Remember what we know, and follow a grain of rice from seed to plate.

steps.title: What we know so far
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 2 and Class 3, what did we find out about keeping healthy?' Good answers: food becomes our body. Soap washes germs off. The heart beats faster when we exercise. Muscles get stronger while we rest and sleep. We get two sets of teeth. Skin, eyes, ears and nose each protect themselves. My body belongs to me. Ask: 'What is one question you still have about health?' Write it down, and see if this lesson answers it.

steps.title: Where did this rice come from?
steps.do: Put a spoonful of uncooked rice in your child's palm. Ask: 'How many people and living things had to help, for this rice to be in your hand?' Let them guess. Then tell the journey, asking at each step 'What does the plant need here?'. A seed, kept from last year's crop or bought, is sown in a nursery bed. The young plants need water from rain or a canal, sunlight, air and nutrients from the soil. Earthworms and tiny soil microbes keep the soil healthy. The farmer ploughs, transplants the seedlings into flooded fields, weeds and watches. The rice ripens and is harvested. Threshing separates the grain from the stalk. Milling takes off the outer husk. The rice is packed, carried by truck, sold by a shopkeeper, bought, washed and cooked. Say: 'In Tamil Nadu, much of the rice grows in the Cauvery delta, around Thanjavur.' Ask: 'Which step was the hardest work? Who did it?' (Often the women who transplant the seedlings by hand, bent over in the water.) Ask: 'Who do you think is paid least along this journey?'

steps.title: Thank-you chain
steps.do: Start Activity a1: a paper chain with one link for each living thing or person on the rice's journey.

steps.title: Start the food-waste count
steps.do: Explain the project. For 6 nights, your family puts all the food it throws away in a separate container and weighs it on a kitchen scale, or counts it in bowls. Peels, seeds and bones go in one column, 'couldn't be eaten'. Leftovers and spoiled food go in another, 'could have been eaten'. Set it up now and do tonight's count.

need: strips of coloured paper, glue or a stapler
a kitchen scale (or a bowl to count with)

days.title: Digestion starts in your mouth
days.goal: Find out that chewing and saliva start digestion, and eat mindfully.

steps.title: Waste count
steps.do: Look at last night's food-waste numbers together and write them in the project table. Ask: 'Was most of it peels, or food we could have eaten?'

steps.title: The sweet roti test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Set up the two cups first. While they wait, your child chews a piece of plain roti or rice for a long time and notices the taste change. Then add the iodine.

steps.title: The one-raisin meal
steps.do: Give your child one raisin, or one grape, or a small piece of jaggery (vellam). Say: 'We're going to eat this as if it's the first one you've ever seen.' Look at it for 30 seconds: the colour, the wrinkles. Smell it. Put it in the mouth without chewing for 20 seconds. Ask: 'What happens?' (Saliva comes.) Chew very slowly, 20 times, noticing the taste. Swallow and feel where it goes. Ask: 'Was that different from how you usually eat?' Say: 'Eating slowly, noticing the taste and stopping when you're full is called mindful eating.'

steps.title: How do you know you're full?
steps.do: Ask: 'How do you know when you're full?' Listen. Say: 'Your stomach stretches as it fills, and it sends messages to your brain. Those messages can take 20 minutes or so. So someone who eats very fast can eat too much before the message arrives.' Ask: 'Do you notice when you're full if you eat in front of a screen?' Ask: 'Are there children who never get to feel full? Why?' (Yes. In India and the world many people don't have enough food, even though the world grows enough for everyone. So hunger is about how food is shared, not only about how much is grown.)

need: plain roti or cooked rice, and the starchy water (kanji) from cooking rice
a raisin, grape or piece of jaggery
tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine antiseptic (from a chemist), two small cups, a spoon, a bowl of warm water

days.title: How much is enough?
days.goal: Look at food waste and ask what happens to it.

steps.title: Waste count
steps.do: Add last night's numbers to the table. Ask: 'Which meal makes the most waste in our house? Why?'

steps.title: Where does wasted food go?
steps.do: Ask: 'When we throw food away, where does it go?' Follow it: the bin, the truck, the dump. Say: 'In a big heap without air, rotting food makes a gas called methane, which warms the planet. And all the water, soil, work and fuel that grew the food were wasted too.' Show the thank-you chain: 'If we waste this rice, we waste every link.' Then: 'In a compost bin, with air, worms and microbes turn scraps back into soil.' Ask: 'Which of our waste could go to compost? Which could have been eaten?' Say: 'The United Nations worked out in 2021 that homes in India throw away about 50 kg of food per person each year.' Ask: 'Is that more or less than you weigh?'

steps.title: Do smaller plates make us eat less?
steps.do: Tell voice v4. A famous food scientist said that smaller plates trick people into eating less. Later, other scientists found serious mistakes in his numbers, and many of his papers were withdrawn. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Worksheet: food and digestion (core)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Ask your child to explain each answer before writing it. For the 'enough' question, accept any honest, reasoned answer.

days.title: Germs and the body's defences
days.goal: Find out how infectious diseases spread and how the body fights back.

steps.title: Waste count
steps.do: Add last night's numbers. Ask: 'Is it going up or down since we started counting? Why?' (Often, just counting makes a family waste less.)

steps.title: Infectious diseases
steps.do: Say: 'An infectious disease is an illness caused by germs that can spread from one living being to another.' Name four kinds of germs: bacteria (they can cause typhoid, cholera and TB), viruses (colds, flu, chickenpox, measles, COVID-19), fungi (ringworm) and tiny parasites (like the one that causes malaria, carried by mosquitoes). Ask: 'How can germs travel?' (Through the air from coughs and sneezes, on dirty hands, in dirty water and food, by insect bites, by touching.) Ask: 'Is a cold infectious? Is a broken leg?' (Yes. No.)

steps.title: The body's walls and soldiers
steps.do: Draw a castle on paper. Say: 'Your body has walls.' Draw them: skin (unbroken skin keeps germs out, which is why we clean cuts), mucus and nose hairs (they trap germs), tears and saliva (they wash away and kill some germs), and stomach acid (it kills many germs in food). Say: 'If germs get past the walls, the soldiers come.' Draw white blood cells: they travel in the blood, find germs and destroy them. All these defences together are called the immune system. Say: 'Fever is part of the fight. A warmer body makes it harder for many germs to grow.' Then ask: 'Why do most people get chickenpox only once?' Let your child guess. Say: 'After a fight, some white blood cells remember that germ. If it comes again, they recognise it at once and destroy it before you get ill. That is called immunity.'

steps.title: Castle tag
steps.do: A quick chasing game. The parent is a germ who tries to touch a cushion (the body). The child is a white blood cell who tags the germ before they reach it. If more people play, some stand in a line as the skin wall and can only shuffle sideways. Play two rounds. In the second round, the white blood cell already 'knows' the germ and starts right next to them, like immunity. Ask: 'Why was round two easier?'

steps.title: Story: The Tikadar Comes in Spring
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). It is told by Bindu, a girl in a Bengal village long ago. Ask the story questions. Ask especially: 'Why didn't Bindu and her brother Mohan fall ill in the summer?' Don't answer for them. Tomorrow's lesson will.

need: paper and pencil for the castle drawing

days.title: Vaccines: teaching the body to remember
days.goal: Learn how vaccines work and how they protect a whole community.

steps.title: Waste count and story recap
steps.do: Add last night's waste numbers. Then ask: 'In the story, what did the tikadar do to Bindu's arm? Why did it protect her?' (He gave her a small dose of smallpox on purpose, so her body learned to beat it and remembered it.)

steps.title: From variolation to vaccines
steps.do: Tell voice v1. For centuries, people in India, China, Africa and Turkey protected themselves against smallpox by variolation, a small dose of smallpox on purpose. Onesimus, an enslaved African man, told people in Boston about it. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to England from Turkey. In 1796, Edward Jenner found a safer way, using a mild cow disease called cowpox. Say: 'A vaccine shows the body a harmless form or a piece of a germ. The white blood cells learn it and remember it, without you getting ill.' Then: 'Smallpox was wiped out from the whole Earth. The last natural case was in 1977. India's last case of polio was a little girl in West Bengal in 2011. Millions of health workers going door to door made that happen.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: How vaccines protect everyone
steps.do: Do Experiment e3, the model town with dice. Before each round, your child guesses how many of the 25 people will fall ill and writes it down. After all three rounds, ask: 'Which round protected the unvaccinated people best? Why?' (Round 2. The vaccinated people broke the chains.)

steps.title: Your own vaccine card
steps.do: Do Activity a3: look at your child's immunisation card together.

need: 25 coins or bottle caps (or squares drawn on paper)

days.title: Medicines: what they do and how to use them safely
days.goal: Learn the rules for medicines and the story of penicillin.

steps.title: Waste count
steps.do: Add last night's waste numbers to the table. Tomorrow is the last count. Ask: 'Which column is bigger so far: could have been eaten, or couldn't?'

steps.title: Medicine-cabinet check (with a grown-up)
steps.do: Do Activity a2: with you, your child reads the labels of medicines at home.

steps.title: Antibiotics and the mould on the melon
steps.do: Ask: 'Will an antibiotic cure a cold?' Listen. Say: 'Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them growing. They do nothing to viruses, so they don't cure a cold or the flu.' Tell voice v3. In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria. Ten years later, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, Norman Heatley and their team made it into a medicine, penicillin. A lab worker, Mary Hunt, found a mouldy melon whose mould made far more penicillin. Ask the voice question. Then explain resistance: 'When antibiotics are used and they are not needed, most bacteria die, but a few tough ones survive and multiply. Then the medicine stops working on them. Doctors call this antibiotic resistance. It is one of the biggest worries in medicine today. So take antibiotics only when a doctor says, exactly as the doctor says.' If there is time, draw a bacterium (a living cell with a wall and their own machinery) next to a virus (a much smaller coat around instructions, with no machinery of their own). Ask: 'What can an antibiotic attack in the virus?' (Nothing.)

steps.title: Worksheet: germs, vaccines and medicines (stretch)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Your child should give reasons for the written items; let them use the castle drawing and the e3 results.

need: the medicines at home, with a grown-up

days.title: Medicines from plants, and a fair test
days.goal: Learn how we find out if a medicine really works, and look at safety around us.

steps.title: Last waste count
steps.do: Add the last night's numbers and total each column. Draw a simple bar chart: one bar per day. Ask: 'What pattern do you see?'

steps.title: The scientist who read old books
steps.do: Tell voice v2. Tu Youyou searched more than 2,000 old Chinese recipes for fever and found one using a plant called sweet wormwood. Her team made a medicine, artemisinin, that has saved millions of people from malaria. Ask the voice question. Say: 'Many medicines started in plants. Aspirin was first made from a substance found in willow bark. Indian healers have used tulsi, neem and turmeric for centuries. But a plant being natural doesn't mean it works or is safe. The only way to know is a fair test.'

steps.title: Design a fair test
steps.do: Ask: 'Someone says drinking a special tea cures colds. How could we find out if that is true?' Let your child suggest ideas first. Then plan it together. You need many people with colds. Split them into two groups by chance, for example by tossing a coin. One group drinks the tea. The other drinks a tea that looks and tastes the same but has nothing special in it, called a placebo. Nobody knows who got which. Count how fast each group gets better. Ask: 'Why must nobody know which tea they got?' (People who expect to feel better often do feel a little better. This is called the placebo effect.) 'Why many people, not just one?' (Colds get better by themselves anyway, and one person can be a fluke.)

steps.title: Safe places, safe choices
steps.do: Ask your child to walk you, in words, from home to the nearest park or shop: 'Where is it safe to play? Where is it not?' (Not on roads, or near open drains, building sites, loose wires or deep water.) Say: 'Last year you named five trusted adults, one for each finger. Who are they?' Add: 'If someone is being hurt, bullied or scared, at home, in the street or online, telling a trusted adult is not telling tales. It keeps people safe.' Then do Worksheet ws3 section A (challenge).

need: the waste table and paper for a bar chart

days.title: Defend the body: game, results and teach it back
days.goal: Share the project, play the game and teach it back.

steps.title: Finish the challenge
steps.do: Finish Worksheet ws3 section B. Talk about the written answers. Accept any well-reasoned answer, and ask: 'What evidence would change your mind?'

steps.title: Project: our food-waste report
steps.do: Your child presents the food-waste report to the family: the table, the bar chart, the pattern, what could have been eaten, and three ideas to waste less (cook less, serve small and take seconds, use leftovers, compost peels). Ask the family to choose one idea to keep.

steps.title: Defend the Body
steps.do: Play the card game g1. After each answer, the player who read the card asks 'How do you know?' On a GERM ATTACK card, everyone stands and shows their defence with their body (a wall, a sneeze into the elbow, a white blood cell gobbling).

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a family member how a vaccine works using the castle drawing, and the four rules for medicines. Then ask the check questions. Add the thank-you chain to the dining-table wall.

experiments.title: The sweet roti test
experiments.question: Does digestion begin before food reaches the stomach?
need: a small piece of plain roti
3 spoons of the starchy water (kanji) poured off cooking rice, cooled
tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine antiseptic from a chemist (a few drops)
two small steel or glass cups
a bowl of warm water, about as warm as a bath
steps: Put about one spoon of kanji in each cup and add one spoon of plain water to each.

Your child spits about a spoonful of saliva into one cup, a little at a time, and stirs. The other cup gets one more spoon of plain water instead. Stand both cups in the bowl of warm water for 15 minutes, because saliva works best at body warmth.

While you wait, your child chews a piece of plain roti for at least 2 minutes without swallowing, noticing the taste every 30 seconds. Ask: 'Has the taste changed?' (Most people find it turns slightly sweet.)
After 15 minutes, a grown-up adds 2 drops of iodine to each cup and stirs. Iodine turns blue-black when there is starch.
Compare the two cups. If both are equally dark, add more saliva to the first cup and wait 10 minutes more.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which cup will turn darker? Why?'
experiments.observe: The roti tastes sweeter after long chewing. The cup with plain water turns dark blue-black. The cup with saliva is lighter, or brownish, because some of the starch has gone.
experiments.why: Rice and roti are full of starch, which is made of long chains of sugar joined together. Starch does not taste sweet. Saliva contains an enzyme called amylase. An enzyme is a substance in the body that speeds up a change. Amylase cuts starch into smaller sugars, which do taste sweet. So digestion begins in the mouth. Iodine shows starch by turning blue-black, so less colour means less starch is left. Chewing well also breaks food into small pieces, so the stomach and gut can digest it more easily.
experiments.safety: Iodine is poisonous to swallow and stains: a grown-up handles it, and nobody eats anything from the test cups. Throw them away and wash the cups.

experiments.title: A model town: how vaccines protect everyone
experiments.question: How can vaccines protect people who aren't vaccinated?
need: 25 coins, buttons or bottle caps (or a 5×5 grid on paper)
steps: Lay the 25 coins in a 5×5 square. Each coin is a person in the town.

Round 1, nobody vaccinated: put a mark next to the middle coin; it's ill. Each turn, for each ill person, roll the die for each neighbour (up, down, left, right): 1 to 4 means the neighbour catches it. Ill people get better after one turn and can't catch it again. Keep going until nobody is ill. Count how many got ill.

Round 2, most vaccinated: turn 18 coins face down, spread across the square. They are vaccinated and can't catch it. Keep the middle coin face up and ill, and 6 others face up. Play again the same way. Count how many unvaccinated people got ill.
Round 3, half vaccinated: turn 12 coins face down, spread out, and play again.
Compare the three counts.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'In round 2, will the unvaccinated people get ill? How many?'
experiments.observe: With nobody vaccinated, the disease usually spreads through most of the town. With most vaccinated, it usually dies out quickly, and many unvaccinated people never catch it, because it can't reach them.
experiments.why: A germ needs a chain of people to travel along. Vaccinated people break the chain. When enough people are protected, the germ can't find new people to infect, so it dies out. This protects babies, very old people and ill people who can't have some vaccines. It is called herd immunity, or community protection. The model is simple. Real diseases spread differently, and how many people need vaccinating depends on the disease. For measles, it is about 19 in every 20.
experiments.safety: No safety worries: this is a game with coins and a die.

experiments.title: Do we waste less when we measure?
experiments.question: How much food does our family throw away, and does counting change it?
need: a kitchen scale (or a bowl to count with)
steps: Put a separate scrap container in the kitchen.
Each night, sort the day's thrown-away food into 'couldn't be eaten' and 'could have been eaten', and weigh or count each.
Write the numbers in a table.
Do this for 6 nights, without trying to change anything at first.
On Day 7, draw a bar chart and look for a pattern.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will we waste more on some days than others? Will counting change how much we waste?'
experiments.observe: Most families find more 'could have been eaten' waste than they expected, and many find it drops once they start counting.
experiments.why: Measuring something often changes how people behave, because they start to notice it. Scientists have to watch out for this in experiments too. Food waste matters because every grain carries the water, soil, work and fuel that grew it. Food that rots in a dump without air makes methane, a gas that warms the planet.

activities.title: Thank-you chain
steps: On each strip, your child writes or draws one link in the rice's journey: soil, rain, sun, earthworms, soil microbes, the seed, the farmer, the women who transplant seedlings, the bullock or tractor, the thresher, the mill worker, the truck driver, the shopkeeper, the person who cooked.
Join the strips into a chain in order.
Add any others they think of: the bees that pollinate other crops, the person who mended the road.
Hang it near where you eat.
Before one meal each day this week, someone touches the chain and thanks one link out loud.
activities.outcome: A paper chain showing that every meal is made by many living things and people.

activities.title: Medicine-cabinet check
steps: A grown-up takes out the medicines; your child does not touch pills or open bottles.
Read each label together: the medicine's name, what it's for, the dose (how much, how often, for which age), and the expiry date.
Sort them: still in date, or expired. A grown-up puts the expired ones aside. Ask your chemist if they take back old medicines. Never pour medicines down a drain.
Make a rule card with your child: 1. Medicines only from a grown-up I trust. 2. The right dose, never more. 3. Never someone else's medicine. 4. Medicines are not sweets, even if they taste sweet.
Check that medicines are stored high up and away from small children.
activities.outcome: A safe medicine shelf and a four-rule card in your child's handwriting.

activities.title: My vaccine card
need: your child's immunisation card (the Mother and Child Protection card or a clinic record)
steps: Look at the card together. Find the names of the vaccines your child had and when: for example BCG (against TB), polio drops, measles-rubella, and others.
For each, ask: 'What disease does this protect against?'
Ask: 'Who gave you these? Where?' (A nurse, an ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife), or a doctor, at a clinic, a hospital or an anganwadi.)
Count how many diseases your child is protected against.
activities.outcome: Your child knows which diseases their own body has been trained to remember.

project.title: Our family food-waste report
steps: Each night for 6 days, weigh or count the food your family throws away, in two columns: 'couldn't be eaten' (peels, bones, seeds) and 'could have been eaten' (leftovers, spoiled food, plate scrapings).
On Day 7, total each column and draw a bar chart, one bar per day.
Find a pattern: which day or meal wasted most? Did counting change anything?
Write three ideas to waste less, and find out where your peels could go (compost pit, a cow, a garden).
Present the report on Day 8 and choose one idea for the family to keep.
project.outcome: A real measurement of your family's food waste, a chart, and one change the family agrees to.

game.title: Defend the Body
rules: Shuffle the cards and deal them face down into one pile.
On your turn, take a card and read the question to the player on your right.
If they answer correctly with a reason, they keep the card as a 'white blood cell'.
If a card says 'GERM ATTACK', every player must name one defence of the body; anyone who can't gives back one card.
When the pile is gone, the player with most white blood cells wins.

cards.back: Vaccinated people around her break the chain, so the germ can't reach her.

voices.who: Onesimus (17th–18th century), West Africa and Boston; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu (1689–1762), England; the tikadars of Bengal; and Edward Jenner (1749–1823), England
voices.idea: Long before vaccines, people in India, China, the Ottoman Empire and many parts of Africa protected themselves against smallpox by variolation: putting a little material from a smallpox sore into a small cut, which usually gave a mild illness and lifelong protection. In Bengal, travelling inoculators called tikadars did this every spring; British doctors wrote about it in the 1760s. Onesimus, an enslaved West African man, told the minister Cotton Mather that he had been inoculated as a child in Africa; in the 1721 Boston smallpox epidemic, Mather and a doctor, Zabdiel Boylston, tried it and far fewer inoculated people died. That same year, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen it in Turkey, had her daughter inoculated in London. In 1796, Edward Jenner showed that cowpox, a mild cattle disease, could protect against smallpox much more safely. The word vaccine comes from 'vacca', Latin for cow.
voices.then: In Boston, many doctors and citizens were furious. Someone threw a lit bomb through Mather's window, but it did not go off. Many refused to believe that an enslaved African could teach them medicine. Jenner's method was also doubted and mocked at first, but it spread quickly.
voices.now: Jenner's work led to all vaccines and is honoured everywhere. Historians now also stress the African, Asian and women's knowledge that came before him, which was often left out of the story. Smallpox was declared wiped out by the World Health Organization in 1980; it is the only human disease ever eradicated.
voices.ask: The usual story starts with Jenner. Where do you think the story should start, and why?

voices.idea: In 1969 Tu Youyou was asked to lead a team in a secret Chinese project searching for a new malaria medicine. She and her team looked through more than 2,000 old recipes from Chinese medicine. A text by Ge Hong, written about 1,600 years ago, described soaking sweet wormwood in cold water. Tu realised that heating might be destroying the active ingredient, so she used a low-temperature method and got an extract that cleared malaria in mice and monkeys. She tested it on herself first. The medicine, artemisinin, is now the main treatment for malaria worldwide.
voices.then: For decades she was little known, even in China. She had no doctorate, had never studied abroad, and the project was secret and credited to the whole team.
voices.now: In 2015 she won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel in science. Artemisinin medicines have saved millions of lives, many of them children in Africa and Asia. Some scientists who worked on the same project have argued that others deserved a share of the credit. Malaria parasites in some places are now becoming resistant to it.
voices.ask: Tu Youyou found the idea in a 1,600-year-old book, but she still tested it carefully. Why wasn't the old book enough on its own?

voices.who: Alexander Fleming (1881–1955), Howard Florey (1898–1968), Ernst Chain (1906–1979), Norman Heatley (1911–2004) and Mary Hunt, UK and USA
voices.idea: In 1928 Fleming noticed that a mould, Penicillium, had killed bacteria on a dish in his London lab. But he couldn't purify it, and stopped working on it. Ten years later, in Oxford, Florey and Chain's team turned it into a medicine. Heatley, a lab scientist without a medical degree, invented the clever apparatus (some made from bedpans and milk churns) to make enough penicillin to test. In 1943, in Peoria, USA, a lab worker named Mary Hunt brought in a mouldy cantaloupe melon from a market; its mould made far more penicillin, and most penicillin made since came from its descendants. She got the nickname 'Mouldy Mary'.
voices.then: Fleming became world-famous, partly through newspapers that loved the story of the lucky dish. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize. Heatley and Hunt were mostly left out.
voices.now: Historians agree penicillin needed all of them. In 1990 Oxford University gave Heatley an honorary doctorate of medicine, the first it had given to a non-doctor in its long history. Penicillin and later antibiotics have saved hundreds of millions of lives, but bacteria resistant to them are now a serious worldwide problem.
voices.ask: Fleming made the first discovery, but others made it work. Who do you think deserves the most credit? Why do we usually remember only one name?

voices.idea: Wansink was a famous food scientist who reported that people eat less from smaller plates, eat more from bottomless soup bowls, and can be nudged into healthy eating with tricks. His findings were widely used in schools and diet advice.
voices.then: From 2016, other scientists checked his papers and found many errors and impossible numbers. He had written a blog post describing how his team kept analysing data until they found something interesting.
voices.now: In 2018, Cornell University found that he had committed academic misconduct, and he resigned. Many of his papers were retracted, which means withdrawn. Whether plate size really changes how much people eat is still debated. Some careful studies find a small effect and others find none. His own results are rejected.
voices.ask: A famous scientist from a top university was wrong. How did other scientists find out? What does that tell you about how science checks itself?

story.title: The Tikadar Comes in Spring
text: My name is Bindu. In the year my brother Mohan turned six, the tikadar came to our village in the spring, as he did every spring, walking from the north with a cloth bag on his shoulder and the dust of a hundred villages on his feet. This was a long time ago, in Bengal, before anyone had heard of vaccines. I was eight. I remember it as clearly as yesterday.

We children ran to see him. He was a thin, quiet man with a sacred thread across his chest and a small silver box he kept tied at his waist. The grown-ups spoke to him with respect, and with something else too. I didn't know the word for it then. Now I would say fear.

Everyone knew why he came. Every few summers, when the heat was at its worst, the smallpox came too. Ma Shitala's visit, the old women called it. It came in through one door and went out through many. It covered children in sores, and it took some of them, and it left others with faces marked for ever, and some who lived could not see afterwards. Our neighbour's boy, Haru, had marks like rain on dust all over his cheeks from the summer I was four.
The tikadar sat under the banyan tree and the mothers brought their children one by one.
My mother stood at the edge of the crowd, holding Mohan's hand very tightly, and did not go forward. I heard my father say to her, low, "Every year you wait."
"Because some of them get ill from it," my mother said. "You know that. Kanak's daughter, two years ago."

It was true. The tikadar's cure was a strange one. He did not stop the smallpox. He gave you smallpox: a little of it, on purpose. Most children who had it from him got a few sores and a fever and were well in a week or two. A very few got ill like the real thing, and once in a while one did not get up again. That was the fear in the grown-ups' faces.
"And how many died in the summer when Haru was ill?" said my father. "How many who had not had the tika?"
My mother did not answer. Then she let go of Mohan's hand, and took mine, and walked us both to the banyan tree.

The tikadar looked at us with kind, tired eyes. He asked what we had eaten and told my mother what we must and must not eat for the coming days. Then he opened his silver box. Inside was a little cotton, and on it, he said, was the dried matter from the sores of a child he had treated last year, far away, who had grown well again. He took a small sharp blade and made two tiny scratches on the outside of my arm, below the shoulder. It stung like an ant bite. He pressed the cotton on, and bound it with a cloth.

"Now," he said, "your body will meet the Mother's fever in a small way, at a time we choose, while you are strong and the weather is cool. It will learn her. And when she comes in the summer, your body will remember."
"How can a body remember?" I asked. My mother hushed me, but the tikadar smiled.
"How do you know your mother's voice in the dark?" he said. "You have heard it before. Bodies are like that too."

In a week I had a fever and nine sores on my arm and one on my chin. Mohan had a few more. We lay on the mat and my mother poured cool water over us and sang, and the old women brought neem leaves, and by the time the mango blossom fell we were well again, with small round scars on our arms.
Then the summer came, and the smallpox came with it.

It came to the potters' houses first, by the tank, and then it walked down our lane. Doors were closed. Fires were lit. You could hear crying at night. Some of the children in our lane had had the tika, and some had not, because their parents had been too frightened or too poor to pay the tikadar.

And here is the thing I have never forgotten. Mohan and I went in and out of the houses where the sickness was. We carried water. We sat with Kanak's youngest, Bela, who had not had the tika and lay burning with fever. We fanned her and gave her water from a little brass cup. We touched everything she touched.
And we did not fall ill.
Not a fever. Not a single sore. It was as if the sickness walked right past us without seeing us.
"It doesn't know us," Mohan whispered to me one night.
"No," I said. I was thinking about the tikadar's words. "We know it."

Bela lived. She was marked on her arms and her back, but not her face, and she could still see. She would sit with me after that on the steps of the tank, and when the tikadar came the next spring, it was Kanak who walked first to the banyan tree, carrying her baby.

I am an old woman now, as I tell you this. They say that in England a doctor has found a gentler way, using a sickness from cows, and that it is coming here. I hope it does. I hope one day no mother ever has to stand at the edge of a crowd and choose between two fears.
But I still have the little round scars on my arm. Sometimes I touch them and think of the summer the sickness walked past me, and the thin man under the banyan tree who taught my body to remember.
story.epiphany: Immunity: the body remembers a germ it has met and beaten, so a small, controlled meeting with it (variolation, and later vaccination) protects against the real disease. The turn is Bindu and Mohan nursing Bela without falling ill: 'It doesn't know us.' 'We know it.' The story also shows the real Indian knowledge of the tikadars, a mother's hard choice between two risks, and protection passing from one family to the next.
ask: What did the tikadar actually do to the children's arms?
Why was Bindu's mother afraid of the tika? Was she right to be afraid?
Why didn't Bindu and Mohan fall ill in the summer?
What did the tikadar mean when he asked how Bindu knew her mother's voice in the dark?
Why do you think Kanak walked first to the banyan tree the next spring?

ideas.idea: Every meal is made by thousands of living things and people.
ideas.more: Soil microbes, earthworms, rain, the sun, farmers, transplanters, millers, drivers and cooks. Use the thank-you chain. Nobody grows their own dinner alone.

ideas.idea: Your immune system remembers germs it has beaten.
ideas.more: After beating a germ, some white blood cells remember it, often for years. Vaccines use this memory: they teach the body to recognise a germ without the danger of the full disease.

ideas.idea: Some protection is shared, not owned.
ideas.more: When enough people are vaccinated, a germ can't travel from person to person. So babies and ill people who can't be vaccinated are protected too. Everyone shares this protection, like clean air.

unknowns: Why does the immune system remember some germs for life (like measles) but others only for a few months or years? Scientists are still working this out.
Can we make vaccines that work against germs that keep changing, like the flu and HIV? Nobody has fully cracked it yet.

How can the world stop bacteria from becoming resistant to all our antibiotics? Scientists are searching for new antibiotics in soil, in the sea, even in old medical texts, and nobody knows yet if we will win the race.
big: If a meal takes thousands of helpers, who owns it?
Is it right that some people throw food away while others are hungry? What could change it?
Should someone be forced to have a vaccine to protect others, or should it be their choice?
Why do we remember one name for a discovery when many people made it happen?
Is a germ an enemy, or just another living thing trying to live?

challenge.hint: Jenner made it much safer in 1796 using cowpox, and 'vaccine' comes from his work. But the idea of protecting people by giving a small dose of smallpox was practised for centuries in India, China, Africa and Turkey, and Onesimus and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to America and England in 1721. Ask: why might the older story have been left out of European books?

No. Many powerful medicines come from plants (artemisinin, aspirin's ancestor from willow), but plants also make deadly poisons, and the right dose matters. Natural or not, a medicine has to be tested fairly. Ask: what's the difference between 'it's natural' and 'it's been tested'?

challenge.q: 'Fleming discovered penicillin by luck, and that's the whole story.'
challenge.hint: Fleming noticed it, and noticing is a skill. But he couldn't make it into a medicine. That took Florey, Chain, Heatley, many lab workers and Mary Hunt's mouldy melon, over 15 years. Ask: why do newspapers like stories of a lone genius and a lucky accident?

perspectives.who: A rice farmer in the Cauvery delta, Tamil Nadu
perspectives.view: A farmer may spend four months growing rice, risking drought, floods and pests, and often gets only part of what you pay in the shop. Ask: what would be a fair share? What would change if everyone knew their farmer's name?

An earthworm eats dead leaves and soil, and leaves behind rich droppings called castings that feed plants. Earthworms help grow your food, though they never eat a grain of it. Ask: how could your family look after the earthworms that help grow your food?

A bacterium that makes you ill is not trying to hurt you. Bacteria are trying to eat, grow and make more of themselves, like every living thing. Your warm body, full of food, happens to be a good place to do it. Ask: does thinking of a germ this way change how you feel about them?

Kang, working at the Christian Medical College in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, found that some vaccines made for rich countries worked less well in Indian children, whose guts face more infections. She helped test Rotavac, an affordable vaccine made in India against rotavirus, a germ that causes deadly diarrhoea in babies. It is now in India's national vaccine programme. In 2019 she became the first Indian woman elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, a famous group of scientists in Britain. Ask: why might a medicine work differently in different places?

perspectives.who: ASHA workers, ANMs and polio vaccinators
perspectives.view: India became polio-free because health workers, many of them women, went door to door, to slums, trains, bus stands and villages, again and again, for years. Ask: who should get the credit for ending polio in India?

books.title: Bread, Bread, Bread
books.author: Ann Morris
books.why: Photographs of bread from around the world, good for thinking about grains and the people who make food.

books.title: How to Make an Apple Pie and See the World
books.author: Marjorie Priceman
books.why: A funny journey round the world to collect every ingredient, showing how many places and people one dish needs.

books.title: Germs Make Me Sick!
books.author: Melvin Berger
books.why: How bacteria and viruses make us ill and how the body fights back.

books.title: I Contain Multitudes
books.author: Ed Yong
books.why: A brilliant adult book about the microbes in and on us, and why most are friends.

check.q: Tell the journey of a grain in five steps, and name two living helpers.
check.a: For example: sowing, growing, harvesting, threshing, milling. Two living helpers: earthworms and soil microbes, or the farmer.

check.q: Why does a roti taste sweet after long chewing?
check.a: Saliva has an enzyme, amylase, that turns starch into sugar. Digestion starts in the mouth.

check.q: What did our food-waste count show, and what will we change?
check.a: Your family's own numbers and chosen idea.

check.q: Name three defences the body has against germs.
check.a: Skin, mucus and nose hairs, tears, stomach acid, white blood cells, fever.
It shows the immune system a harmless form or piece of a germ, so it learns it and remembers it.

check.q: How do vaccines protect people who can't have them?
check.a: Vaccinated people break the chain, so the germ can't reach them (community or herd protection).

check.q: Why shouldn't you take antibiotics for a cold?
check.a: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work on bacteria. Using antibiotics when they are not needed helps resistant bacteria spread.

check.q: Who else, apart from Jenner, should be remembered for protecting people from smallpox?
check.a: The tikadars of India, Onesimus, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, the vaccinators who ended smallpox.
